stories.title: Ambush in South Sudan kills peacekeeping troops
stories.summary: Two UN peacekeepers killed in South Sudan ambush as fears grow of the country relapsing into civil war. An ambush has killed two United Nations peacekeepers in South Sudan. The UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) said in a statement issued on Monday that armed men had ambushed a patrol as it travelled toward Pajut in Jonglei state. The attack comes as fears persist that the country risks sliding into a full-scale civil war. The identities and nationalities of those killed have not yet been disclosed. Three other peacekeepers were wounded, along with two South Sudanese police officers and two civilian staff attached to the mission. The UN peacekeeping mission said it deployed a “Quick Reaction Force” to secure the area and support the emergency response. “Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel, who are serving to support peace in South Sudan, is unacceptable,” Anita Kiki Gbeho, the head of the mission, said. Numerous attacks on humanitarian workers have been recorded this year as the prospect of full-blown civil war rises, but violence against peacekeepers is rare. UN figures show more than 450 attacks on humanitarian workers and assets between January and July, more than double last year’s total for the same period. At least 36 humanitarian workers and contractors were killed, surpassing the 31 killed across 2025. The violence is playing out against months of grinding conflict between government troops and forces loyal to opposition leader Riek Machar.

stories.title: Ceasefire monitoring mission arrives in Democratic Republic of Congo
stories.summary: Fighting persists in the mineral-rich region despite ceasefire agreements. A monitoring mission has been deployed in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to verify the formal ceasefire between the DRC’s army and M23 rebels said to be backed by Rwanda. The United Nations and government sources said on Monday that the monitoring team had arrived to track the progress of the Qatari-mediated truce. Despite the agreement to end the hostilities, fighting has continued on the ground. The UN said that the mission had deployed to Minembwe, located in the country’s mineral-rich South Kivu province, where intense fighting has persisted in recent months. The Swiss government announced on Sunday that the DRC and M23 had agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after closed-door negotiations, and that a mission would be deployed to verify violations of the ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar in July 2025. The mission is composed of members of the Congolese government and M23, as well as observers from member countries of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR). Local journalists reported that the UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO) provided logistical support for the deployment. The mission will visit Uvira, from where the M23 withdrew in January, as well as Kalehe, where fighting has been reported in recent weeks. Multiple armed groups have fought over the DRC’s mineral-abundant eastern provinces, including the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and M23, which seized swathes of territory and advanced on Goma, the capital of the North Kivu province, last year. Peace efforts led by Qatar and the United States have sought to end the crisis, leading to the signing of two separate accords. DRC President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame – whose country has been accused of backing the M23 rebels – signed a “historic” peace and economic agreement in December aimed at ending fighting, five months after the two agreed to a ceasefire.

stories.title: Malaysia’s PKR faces existential threat as disenchanted veterans drift to splinter party Bersama
stories.summary: PKR faces a crisis as many veterans and leaders, including former deputy president Rafizi Ramli, have left to join the new Parti Bersama Malaysia, causing internal challenges and membership losses. Bersama has gained about 29,200 members since May 2025, including 25% from PKR, and appeals to voters similar to PKR, impacting election results in Johor state. Disenchanted former PKR members see Bersama as a platform to continue reform efforts, criticising PKR for focusing on self-preservation and alliances with former rivals, while PKR struggles with leadership uncertainty. While leaders of Malaysia’s ruling Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) took stock of its uncertain political future at the Melaka International Trade Centre on Aug 15, its former deputy president, Rafizi Ramli, was in a more festive mood. At a suburban bungalow just 20 minutes away, Rafizi, who now leads the nascent Parti Bersama Malaysia, was stirring a large pot of asam pedas – the sour and spicy fish stew popular in the southern state and Johor. Rafizi was attending a party get-together ahead of the Melaka state election. But with 1990s songs playing in the background, the gathering felt more akin to a Malay “kenduri”, or a feast, than a political event. “We want the Malaysian multiracial vibe, and I kind of like this actually,” said the former economy minister. With around 350 guests clad in Bersama yellow, the atmosphere was festive. It was the complete opposite to the solemn and introspective mood at PKR’s four-day national congress. There, the introspection comes as PKR grapples with its most significant challenge since taking over Putrajaya in 2022 – suffering major defeats in recent state elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. Added to this crisis, top leaders have also followed Rafizi to Bersama, including former MPs Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad and Wong Chen.

stories.title: Drying springs in Arizona jeopardize the future of a key Navajo tradition
stories.summary: For centuries, Navajo shepherds have herded sheep in Arizona's mountains. Now, springs they rely on are drying up, putting a mainstay of the tribe's culture at risk.
